summary: Discusses issues in giving the ECN field in the IP header meanings other than those in RFC 3168. It sets requirements so such alternative uses can coexist safely with routers that follow the original behavior. This is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4774 sets requirements for proposals that give the IP ECN field a different meaning. A proposal must explain how routers recognize that meaning and how its traffic remains fair when older routers are on the path.

questions: can the ecn field be redefined
what happens when an old router sees alternate ecn traffic
what is the ce codepoint in ecn
subtitle: Requirements for changing what the IP congestion-notification bits mean without confusing older routers.

tldr.problem: Proposals to give the IP ECN field new meanings must account for routers that still use the original ECN rules or do not use ECN.
tldr.mechanism: A proposal must explain how packets signal the new meaning, how old routers affect performance, and how traffic will coexist fairly; the RFC describes three deployment approaches.
tldr.outcome: Specifications for alternate ECN meanings must address the issues raised and meet the coexistence requirements. RFC 4774 was updated by RFC 6040.

today: RFC 4774 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 124) published in November 2006. It was updated by RFC 6040.

sections.title: Why Alternate ECN Needs Rules
sections.content:
RFC 3168 defines the default meaning of the Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) field in IP packets. Other proposals use the field to signal different congestion information, including proposals for real-time traffic and congestion control.

Routers and hosts cannot all be assumed to change at once. Some older routers may apply the default ECN behavior, may not use ECN, or may be difficult to update. RFC 4774 describes issues that a specification for alternate meanings must consider.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing the ECN bits affects traffic that crosses routers with different software and rules. A new proposal must explain how the change works alongside the original meaning.

sections.title: Questions Every Proposal Must Answer
sections.content:
The RFC groups the design questions into four areas: how routers identify the ECN meaning for a packet; what happens when older routers are present; whether alternate traffic competes fairly with other traffic; and how the scheme performs when all routers understand it.

A proposal may signal the new meaning through a Diffserv codepoint, but the RFC does not require that method. Other methods, including out-of-band signaling, are possible. The same deployment and coexistence concerns apply whichever signal is used.
sections.plainLanguage: A proposal must explain how routers know which rules to apply, what older routers do, and whether other traffic still gets a fair share.

sections.title: Three Ways to Handle Older Routers
sections.content:
An older router that uses default ECN may mark an alternate-ECN packet with the Congestion Experienced (CE) codepoint. If the sender ignores that mark, it may keep sending at the same rate and take capacity from competing traffic. A router that does not use ECN may instead drop packets, so a sender must also consider drops.

The RFC describes three approaches: restrict the alternate semantics to enclosed environments; verify that every router on the path supports them; or define the semantics to coexist fairly with old routers. Path verification can be difficult when routes change, and IP options can reduce performance on routers optimized for packets without options.
sections.plainLanguage: Older routers may mark or drop packets without understanding the new rules. A design must either keep traffic away from those routers, check the path, or respond fairly to their signals.

sections.title: Rules for Fair Coexistence
sections.content:
For compatibility with default-ECN routers, a CE mark of 11 must reach the receiver unless the packet is dropped. The receiving transport must respond to that mark in a way that is friendly to flows using conformant congestion control.

For compatibility with default-ECN endpoints, a packet marked 00 must not be changed to 01, 10 or 11 when a router cannot tell whether it uses default semantics. A packet marked 01 should not be changed to 10, and vice versa, to avoid interference with ECN nonce use.
sections.plainLanguage: A congestion mark must reach the receiver, and the sender must react to it. Routers must also avoid changing codepoints in ways that confuse endpoints using the original rules.

sections.title: Evaluation and Conclusion
sections.content:
Even when all routers understand an alternate meaning, a proposal must consider false feedback from receivers, fair competition with other traffic, interactions with edge-to-edge ECN, and packet tunnels. The RFC leaves the general evaluation criteria to each proposal.

The RFC adds no new Internet mechanisms and says it introduces no new security considerations. A specification for alternate ECN semantics must clearly address the issues in this document and satisfy the requirements for coexistence with competing traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Proposers must also consider misleading feedback and tunnels, even on a path where every router understands the new meaning. The specification must explain these choices and satisfy the fairness rules.

items.title: Enclosed use
items.text: Treat the alternate meaning as unsafe for the global Internet.

items.title: Check the path
items.text: Verify that every router understands and accepts the alternate meaning.

items.title: Coexist
items.text: Define behavior that remains fair when older routers are present.
